extracted.intended_audience: authors, educators, librarians, scholars, and general readers concerned with disability representation in children's literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for how disability is depicted in children's and juvenile literature — what counts as harmful vs. positive representation and how authors/educators should approach portrayal and teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate and authentic representation
rubrics_metrics.description: When authors write books with characters who have disabilities as the main characters, they have a responsibility to write books that are "accurate and authentic" to the experiences of disabled people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as an ethical responsibility (Purkiss). Guidance implies researching lived experience, avoiding invented or sensationalized depictions, and centering authenticity rather than assumptions. Examples: avoid creating situations or character reactions that are inconsistent with real disabled people's experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray disability as part of the character, not the entire identity / multidimensional characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Authentic disability representation portrays disability as a part of the character, rather than making it their entire identity; present characters with a disability as multidimensional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kleekamp & Zapata and Rieger & McGrail recommend showing strengths and weaknesses, varied traits, and life beyond the disability. Anti-patterns: making difference the only defining trait, flattening the character to a single characteristic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let disabled characters' voices tell the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature disabled characters in ways that have their voices tell the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use point-of-view, first-person narration, or ensure a character agency in narration so the disabled character's perspective is foregrounded. Anti-patterns: telling disabled characters' stories only through non-disabled narrators or speaking for them without accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Position readers to not take disabled characters for granted (normalize, avoid tokenism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present disabled characters in ways that position readers to accept them as part of the social world rather than as curiosities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normalize presence and participation in everyday activities; avoid tokenistic inclusion where a character exists only to represent disability without integration into plot or community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray authentic relationships for disabled characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Disabled characters should have authentic relationships rather than being isolated or merely inspirational objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show friendships, family dynamics, romance, conflict and ordinary interactions. Anti-patterns: depicting disabled characters only as inspirational for others or without believable social ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid harmful stereotypes and tropes (pitiful, evil, superhero, burden)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically prevalent stereotypes include characters portrayed as pitiful/pathetic, evil or superhero-like, a burden, or incapable of participating fully in life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce disabled characters to these tropes. Examples cited (Blaska) illustrate these negative archetypes. Evaluate characters for complexity rather than stereotyped roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use disability primarily as a metaphor or plot device for protagonist development
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every disability has to be a 'metaphor for a protagonist's development'; disability should not be used merely to advance plot or symbolize other themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using disability to signify moral insight, racial redemption (e.g., blindness as 'seeing beyond' prejudice), or as a device that exists mainly to change the protagonist rather than reflecting lived experience. Anti-pattern: disabilities that exist solely to teach non-disabled characters lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid patronizing, offensive, vague, or unclear language
rubrics_metrics.description: Language describing disabled characters should not be patronizing or offensive; overly vague or unclear descriptions lead to inaccurate depictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use respectful, specific terminology appropriate to the condition and context. Historical examples show patronizing/offensive descriptors and vague depictions that reinforce stereotypes. Consult contemporary disability-preferred language and sensitivity readers where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid moralizing disability as punishment, divine lesson, or test (the 'School of Pain' / saintliness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disability should not be framed as an opportunity presented by God to learn moral lessons, nor should characters be depicted as saintly suffering as moral exemplars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Katy in What Katy Did (disability as 'School of Pain') and Tiny Tim portrayed as saintly; these frameworks make disability a moralized plot element rather than an aspect of lived experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'othering' and hierarchical portrayals / power imbalances
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not portray disabled characters as the 'other' at the bottom of social hierarchies or define relationships primarily by power imbalances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses of Andersen's tales show disabled characters positioned low in social order; modern portrayals should avoid reinforcing societal hierarchies and power differentials that demean disabled people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid romanticization, infantilization, or depicting withdrawal from the world
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not romanticize or infantilize disabled characters, nor consistently depict them as retreating from society or avoiding the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical patterns (1940–1970 books) included romanticizing, infantilizing, or portraying disabled characters as avoiding normal life. Aim for realistic portrayals of agency and participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent a variety of disabilities, including hidden disabilities; avoid overrepresentation/misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Include diverse types of disabilities (physical, sensory, cognitive, emotional, 'hidden' disabilities) and avoid skewed overrepresentation of certain conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: rising portrayals of 'hidden disabilities' like extreme shyness or dyslexia; beware of historical overrepresentation of blindness used for plot reasons. Authors/editors should broaden representation to reflect population diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use nuanced narrative techniques for complex or sensitive situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex portrayals (e.g., sexual assault of a disabled character) benefit from nuanced techniques such as multiple-perspective narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Erika Tamar's Fair Game uses multiple perspectives to handle a sensitive storyline. Employ narrative form and craft choices that responsibly convey complexity rather than simplifying trauma or agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include educational follow-up (discussion/activities) to improve understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Educators may improve student understanding of disability with follow-up discussion or activities and stories that portray characters with disabilities accurately, realistically, and positively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using books in classrooms, pair reading with guided discussion, activities, or curricula that contextualize representation and counter stereotypes; this amplifies positive effects on acceptance and empathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing disabled people to impersonal groups or oversimplified categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not depict disabled people only as impersonal groups or reduce them to a few oversimplified categories (e.g., 'the blind', 'the deaf').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 19th-century literature often reduced disabled characters to five oversimplified categories. Modern writing should individualize characters and avoid aggregate or dehumanizing group labels.
